topics.title: Series and parallel resistance
topics.summary: Resistances in series add; in parallel, the total is smaller than the smallest one.

lensNotes.circuit: Series parts share a current; parallel parts share a voltage. Most resistor networks reduce to a single resistance by combining pairs from the inside out.
lensNotes.math: Series resistances add; parallel conductances (1/R) add. Product over sum, R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂), is 1/(1/R₁ + 1/R₂) rewritten for two resistors, and a parallel pair is always smaller than either one.

prerequisiteNotes.ohms_law: Each series and parallel rule comes from applying V = IR to every resistor: in series the voltages add at one current; in parallel the currents add at one voltage.
prerequisiteNotes.si_prefixes: Resistances come as 4.7 kΩ or 220 Ω; adding and combining them means working comfortably across prefixes.

goals: Find the total resistance of resistors in series, and of resistors in parallel
Reduce a series-parallel network to one resistance by combining pairs from the inside out
Tell from a schematic which parts are in series and which are in parallel, by tracing the nodes their ends connect to
Explain why adding a resistor in parallel always lowers the total resistance, whatever its value
topics.intuition: A resistor added in series is one more part the same current must pass through, so resistance goes up; a resistor added in parallel is one more path for current between the same two nodes, so resistance goes down, below the smallest branch.
topics.why: In a series chain there is only one path, so the same current flows through every part (charge cannot leave the chain between them). Each part drops I·R, and the drops add: V = I·(R1 + R2). In parallel, both ends of every branch sit on the same two nodes, so every branch has the same voltage across it and carries its own current, V / R. The currents add, so the conductances 1/R add. An extra branch only adds current at the same voltage, so the combination's resistance is below the smallest branch.
topics.explanation: Ohm's law, V = I·R, relates one resistor's voltage and current. Analyzing a circuit with several resistors starts with finding the single resistance they are equivalent to. Two parts are in series when they are joined end to end at a node with nothing else connected to that node. They carry the same current, and their resistances add: 1 kΩ + 2.2 kΩ = 3.2 kΩ. Two parts are in parallel when both their ends connect to the same two nodes. A node is one piece of metal: every wire joined together, however it is drawn. Parallel parts have the same voltage across them, and for two of them R = R1·R2 / (R1 + R2), product over sum. For more, add the reciprocals: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Two useful checks: a parallel combination is always smaller than its smallest resistor, and n equal resistors in parallel give R / n. A mixed network reduces from the inside out: combine one series or parallel pair, redraw it as a single resistor, and repeat until one is left. Judge series or parallel by where the ends connect, never by how the parts are laid out on the page.

workedExample.problem: R1 = 1 kΩ is in series with the parallel pair R2 = 2.2 kΩ and R3 = 4.7 kΩ. Find the total resistance, and the current a 5 V supply drives through the network.
steps: Start inside, with the parallel pair: R2 ∥ R3 = (2.2 kΩ × 4.7 kΩ) / (2.2 kΩ + 4.7 kΩ) = 10.34 kΩ² / 6.9 kΩ = 1.50 kΩ.
Check with conductances: 1 / 2.2 kΩ = 0.455 mS and 1 / 4.7 kΩ = 0.213 mS; 0.455 mS + 0.213 mS = 0.667 mS, and 1 / 0.667 mS = 1.50 kΩ. It is smaller than 2.2 kΩ, the smaller branch, as it must be.
Now R1 is in series with that 1.50 kΩ: R = 1 kΩ + 1.50 kΩ = 2.50 kΩ.
Current from the supply: I = 5 V / 2.50 kΩ = 2.00 mA.

The pair shares one voltage: 2.00 mA × 1.50 kΩ = 3.00 V across both R2 and R3. So I2 = 3.00 V / 2.2 kΩ = 1.36 mA and I3 = 3.00 V / 4.7 kΩ = 0.64 mA. The smaller resistor takes the larger current, and 1.36 mA + 0.64 mA = 2.00 mA, the whole supply current.
R1 carries the full 2.00 mA and drops 2.00 mA × 1 kΩ = 2.00 V; 2.00 V + 3.00 V = 5 V, the supply.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 5 "Series and Parallel Circuits", section "Simple series circuits"
sources.note: A series chain has one path, so it shares one current, and its resistances and voltage drops add.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 5 "Series and Parallel Circuits", section "Simple parallel circuits"
sources.note: Parallel branches share one voltage, branch currents add, and the reciprocal formula gives a total below the smallest branch.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 7 "Series-Parallel Combination Circuits", section "Analysis technique"
sources.note: Reducing a mixed network one series or parallel group at a time, redrawing after each step.

templates.prompt: Resistors of {R1} and {R2} are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
templates.explanation: In series the same current flows through both, so their voltages add, and so do their resistances: R = {R1} + {R2} = {answer}.
hints: In series, the same current flows through every resistor.
Series resistances add: R = R1 + R2.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the parallel formula. Resistances in series add.

templates.prompt: Resistors of {R1} and {R2} are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
templates.explanation: In parallel the conductances add: 1/R = 1/{R1} + 1/{R2}, so R = R1·R2 / (R1 + R2) = {answer}. It is always smaller than the smaller resistor.
hints: Parallel resistors share the same voltage; their currents add.
Use R = R1·R2 / (R1 + R2) (product over sum).

misconceptions.feedback: That's the series total. In parallel the current has two paths, so the total resistance goes down, not up.
You have the product; divide it by the sum: R = R1·R2 / (R1 + R2).
The average is too big: a parallel pair is always below the smaller resistor. Use product over sum, R1·R2 / (R1 + R2).

followUps.prompt: Why is a parallel pair always less than the smaller resistor alone?

choices.text: The second resistor adds another path, so at the same voltage more current flows than through the smaller one alone
choices.feedback: Right: more current for the same voltage means less resistance, R = V / I.

choices.text: The bigger resistor blocks current, which pulls the total down
choices.feedback: The bigger resistor doesn't block anything; it carries its own extra current. That extra current is what lowers the total.

choices.text: The current splits, so each resistor has less voltage across it
choices.feedback: Parallel parts share the same voltage. The current splits, and the total is more than either branch.

choices.text: Parallel resistance is the average of the two
choices.feedback: The average would sit between them. Adding a path can only add current, so the total must be below the smaller value.

followUps.explanation: Put a voltage V across the pair. The smaller resistor alone would draw V / R_small; the second one draws extra current on top. More current at the same voltage means less resistance, so V / I_total is below R_small. That's why conductances (1/R) add in parallel.

templates.prompt: {R1} is in series with the parallel combination of {R2} and {R3}. What is the total resistance?
templates.explanation: Reduce the parallel pair first: {R2} ∥ {R3} = {Rp}. Then add the series resistor: {R1} + {Rp} = {answer}.
hints: Work from the inside out: combine the parallel pair first.
R2 ∥ R3 = R2·R3 / (R2 + R3), then add R1.

misconceptions.feedback: R2 and R3 are in parallel, not series. Combine them with product over sum before adding R1.

followUps.prompt: Why do you combine R2 and R3 before adding R1?

choices.text: R2 and R3 share both ends, so together they act as one resistor, and only that pair carries all of R1's current
choices.feedback: Right: R1's current reaches the junction and splits between R2 and R3, so R1 is in series with the pair.

choices.text: You always combine from right to left
choices.feedback: Position on the page doesn't matter; connections do. You can add R1 in series only with something that carries all of R1's current.

choices.text: R1 is in series with R2 alone, so you could add those first
choices.feedback: R1 and R2 meet at a node that R3 also connects to, so R1's current splits there: R1 isn't in series with R2 alone.

choices.text: Parallel resistors must always be combined last
choices.feedback: There's no fixed order. Find groups that carry one current (series) or share both ends (parallel), innermost first.

followUps.explanation: Two parts are in series only when all of one's current goes through the other. R1's current splits between R2 and R3, so R1 is in series with the pair, not with either one. Reduce the pair to one resistor, then add R1. It's the same reading skill as the schematic problems in this topic.

templates.prompt: A {R1} resistor is connected across a supply. You add a second resistor of {R2} in parallel with it. What happens to the total resistance the supply sees?

choices.text: It goes down, below {R1}
choices.feedback: Right: a parallel path always gives the current another way through, so the total falls below the smallest resistor.

choices.text: It goes up to {R1} + {R2}
choices.feedback: That would be series. In parallel you add a second path for current, which lowers the resistance.

choices.text: It stays at {R1}, because the larger resistor barely matters
choices.feedback: A large parallel resistor changes the total only a little, but it always lowers it.

choices.text: It becomes the average of the two
choices.feedback: Parallel resistance is product over sum, which is always below the smaller value, not the average.

templates.explanation: Adding any resistor in parallel adds a path for current, so the supply delivers more current at the same voltage: the total resistance drops below {R1}.
hints: Does a parallel resistor add a new path for current, or make the existing path longer?

templates.prompt: Resistors of {R1}, {R2}, and {R3} are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
templates.explanation: Conductances add in parallel: 1/R = 1/{R1} + 1/{R2} + 1/{R3}, so R = {answer}. It is smaller than the smallest resistor.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the series total. In parallel the result is smaller than the smallest resistor.

templates.prompt: {n} identical {R} resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
templates.explanation: For n equal resistors in parallel, the total is R/n = {R}/{n} = {answer}.
hints: Each extra path carries the same current.

misconceptions.feedback: That's n resistors in series. In parallel it's R/n.

templates.prompt: {n} identical {R} resistors are connected in parallel. You add one more {R} resistor in parallel with them. What happens to the total resistance?

feedback.up: Adding resistors raises the resistance only in series, where the current must pass through every one. In parallel each one is another path between the same two nodes, so the same voltage now drives current through one more path at once.
feedback.same: Every resistor in parallel has the full voltage across it and carries its own current, however many are already there. The total resistance is that voltage divided by the total current, R = V/I_total, and the new path adds its current to I_total.

templates.explanation: For n equal resistors in parallel, the total is R / n: {before} → {after}. Each extra path adds current at the same voltage, so the total falls. That's why a supply delivers more current as more lamps are switched on in parallel.
hints: Does the new resistor make the current's path longer, or give it another path?
templates.noDrawing: the number of resistors changes from problem to problem, so no single drawing fits

templates.prompt: A circuit calls for {Rt} (within 2%), which is not a standard E12 value. Make it from two E12 resistors, each between 100 Ω and 1 MΩ, connected in parallel between A and B.
templates.explanation: A parallel pair is always below its smaller resistor, so both must be above {Rt}. Start with R1 a little above the target, say the next E12 value up, and solve 1/R2 = 1/{Rt} − 1/R1, that is R2 = R1·{Rt}/(R1 − {Rt}). Round R2 to E12 and check R1·R2/(R1 + R2). If it misses by more than 2%, move R1 up one step and try again. For example, 3.0 kΩ = 3.3 kΩ ∥ 33 kΩ: the large resistor trims the smaller one down a little. The closer R1 is to the target, the larger R2 must be.
hints: Can a parallel pair ever come out larger than either of its resistors?
Pick R1 just above the target, then R2 = R1·Rt/(R1 − Rt); round to E12 and check.

followUps.prompt: Why must both resistors be larger than {Rt}?

choices.text: Each resistor adds a path for current, so the pair is always below the smaller of the two
choices.feedback: Right: at the same voltage the two currents add, so the pair passes more current than either alone and its resistance is lower than both.

choices.text: Parallel resistances add, so each one must be a part of the total
choices.feedback: In parallel the conductances (1/R) add, not the resistances. Each extra path lowers the total.

choices.text: One can be below {Rt} if the other is large enough to make up the difference
choices.feedback: No second resistor can raise the total: it only adds another path. With one resistor below {Rt}, the pair is below {Rt} too.

choices.text: The larger resistor carries more of the current, so it must be above the target
choices.feedback: Both see the same voltage, so the larger resistor carries less current (I = V/R), not more.

followUps.explanation: Both resistors have the same voltage across them, and each carries its own current. The currents add, so at that voltage the pair passes more current than either resistor alone: its resistance is below both. To land on {Rt}, both parts have to start above it.

templates.prompt: A {V} battery feeds a resistor network: R1 = {R1} from the battery to node a, R2 = {R2} from node a to ground, R3 = {R3} from node a to node b, and R4 = {R4} from node b to ground. When the network is healthy, the battery delivers {h0}, node a sits at {h1}, and node b at {h2}. One resistor has failed open or shorted. Which fault explains the readings below?

probes.label: Current from the battery (ammeter in the battery lead)

faults.feedback: An open R2 would remove one of the two paths from node a to ground. The battery would see more resistance, so its current would fall and both nodes would rise, with node b still below node a.
faults.why: The battery current fell and both nodes rose, with node b still below node a, so current still flows through R3 and R4. Losing the R2 path does exactly that: the resistance from a to ground rises from R2 ∥ (R3 + R4) to R3 + R4.

faults.feedback: An open R3 would cut node b off from node a, so node b would fall to 0 V (R4 still ties it to ground). With a path lost, the battery current would fall and node a would rise.
faults.why: Node b reads 0 V while the battery current fell and node a rose. The network's resistance went up, so a path was lost rather than shorted, and with node b dead the lost link is R3.

faults.feedback: An open R4 would stop the current in R3, so R3 would drop nothing and node b would read the same as node a. With a path lost, the battery current would fall and node a would rise.
faults.why: Node b reads the same as node a, so R3 has no voltage across it. The battery current fell, so the network's resistance rose: R3 carries no current because the R3–R4 path is broken at R4.

faults.feedback: A shorted R3 would join nodes a and b, so they would read the same. The second path would shrink to R4 alone, so the battery current would rise and node a would fall.
faults.why: Nodes a and b read the same, yet the battery current rose: the network's resistance fell. A short across R3 joins a to b and leaves R4 as the whole second path to ground.

faults.feedback: A shorted R4 would pull node b to 0 V and leave R3 alone as the second path from node a, so the battery current would rise and node a would fall.
faults.why: Node b reads 0 V while the battery current rose and node a fell: the network's resistance went down. A short at R4 does that. An open R3 would also leave node b at 0 V, but it would raise the resistance and lower the current.

templates.explanation: The battery sees R_eq = R1 + R2 ∥ (R3 + R4) = {Req}, so it delivers {V} / {Req} = {h0}. An open removes a path, so R_eq rises and the battery current falls; a short removes resistance, so R_eq falls and the current rises. The battery current tells you which kind of fault it is. Node a moves the opposite way, because R1 drops more when more current flows through it. Node b then locates the fault: node b at 0 V means it has lost its link to node a or is shorted to ground; node b equal to node a means R3 has no voltage across it, so either it carries no current (R4 open) or it is shorted.
hints: For each fault, does the resistance the battery sees go up or down? That tells you which way the battery current moves.
Node b reading the same as node a means R3 has no voltage across it: either it carries no current, or it is shorted.

followUps.prompt: Suppose R4 opens. R3 is still in place, yet node b then reads the same as node a. Why?

choices.text: R3's far end now leads nowhere, so R3 carries no current and drops V = I·R3 = 0; both its ends sit at node a's voltage
choices.feedback: Right: a resistor only drops voltage while current flows through it. With R4 gone, R3 is a dead end.

choices.text: R3 is now in parallel with R2, so it has the same voltage as node a
choices.feedback: R3 is not in parallel with R2: its far end, node b, connects to nothing but the voltmeter. Node b reads like node a because R3 carries no current and so drops nothing.

choices.text: With R4 gone the battery current rises, and the extra current lifts node b
choices.feedback: Opening R4 removes a path, so the resistance the battery sees rises and its current falls. Node b matches node a because no current flows in R3, not because more current flows.

choices.text: Node b is floating, so the meter shows whatever voltage it had before the fault
choices.feedback: A node joined to nothing would not keep its old voltage; a meter would show a small, drifting reading. Node b is still joined to node a through R3; with no current in R3, it simply reads node a's voltage.

followUps.explanation: Ohm's law sets the voltage across R3 from the current through it: V = I·R3. Healthy, R3 and R4 carry the same current (they are in series), and R3 drops part of node a's voltage. Open R4 and that series path has no way back to ground, so the current in R3 drops to zero (the voltmeter's 10 MΩ draws next to nothing) and so does its voltage: node b reads node a's voltage. This is why a resistor reading equal voltages at both ends points at an open somewhere in its series path, or at a short across the resistor itself.
